#1338. Pregnancy rewires the brain — scientists are finally mapping it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers are striving to understand the massive changes in the brain that occur during pregnancy.Credit: Getty

Pregnancy floods the brain with hormones and remodels brain circuits on a scale rivalled only by the neural transformation that occurs during adolescence. Yet there is a lack of information about how a healthy brain changes during pregnancy, because of past worries about the safety of scanning expectant mothers.

How pregnancy reshapes the brain throughout life

How pregnancy reshapes the brain throughout life

Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented on 17 November at the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington DC, could help to explain why some people develop depression during and after pregnancy, and how they develop other maternal mental-health conditions. These conditions are the leading driver of pregnancy-related deaths in the United States.

It wasn’t until 2024 that researchers reported the first detailed map of a human brain during pregnancy1, after performing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on one woman at 26 timepoints from 3 weeks before conception until 2 years after delivery. The American College of Radiology endorsed the safety of scanning the brains of pregnant people for research purposes that same year.

“Over 80% of women worldwide will experience pregnancy at least once in their lifetimes,” so it’s “imperative” that physicians spot signs of abnormalities early enough to treat conditions such as postpartum depression, said Hannah Grotzinger, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, during a presentation at the meeting. (Grotzinger was also a co-author of the 2024 study.)

Building on the earlier mapping study, Grotzinger and her colleagues expanded the effort to see whether those patterns hold across several people. They tracked six first-time mothers, two second-time mothers and five female participants who were not pregnant. From before conception to one year after birth, each participant underwent up to 30 MRI scans and blood draws.

How does the brain react to birth control? A researcher scanned herself 75 times to find out

How does the brain react to birth control? A researcher scanned herself 75 times to find out

The larger cohort confirmed the shifts first seen in the 2024 map. In first-time mothers, total brain volume had dropped by roughly 3.5% by the time they gave birth. Grey-matter volume was reduced in nearly every region of the brain’s outer layer, or cortex, particularly in areas linked to social cognition. A brain structure called the pallidum, which regulates movement and motivation, was a rare exception: it grew during gestation, when a baby was growing in the womb. The researchers also found that the volume of cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that surrounds and flows through the brain and spinal cord to provide cushioning and nutrients, increased by 11% during gestation.

Second-time mothers showed a similar pattern, but across only about half of their cortical regions. There was no substantial shift in cerebrospinal-fluid volume, suggesting that a first pregnancy has a bigger impact on the brain, Grotzinger said, although she cautioned that more data are needed to confirm these findings given the small sample size.

Such drastic changes to the brain are part of a typical pregnancy and are “not something to be scared of”, says Liisa Galea, a neuroscientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, Canada.

The researchers also observed between the first and second trimester an increase in blood flow in the brain, which peaked around 21 weeks into pregnancy and tapered off near birth. The exception was a participant who developed pre-eclampsia, a serious pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure; the blood flow in their brain remained lower overall throughout gestation, compared with that in other participants, and they had less of a reduction in grey matter.

#1336. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. Or, finally, that it’s 4-2-3-1 with the trident of Rashford, Tielemans and Bruno.

Carrick’s team may look like a dog’s dinner but it has at least provoked plenty of debate.

Diego Simeone weighs in on Julian Alvarez, Michael Carrick & tonight's clash vs Manchester United 👀 https://t.co/1E0H7mkFYn

You can read more about Aljoe’s skill here.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young think Ayden Heaven will start at left-back, Dalot at right-back and Yoro moving in to the centre off the right. They also believe Bruno Fernandes will start on the right with Tielemans pushed higher than Baleba and Andrey Santos.

From their victory over Alaves, Koke, whose mother has died, Le Normand, Lookman and David drop out for Hancko, Lee Kang-in, Baena and Alvarez.

Though Carrick has picked three centre-backs, I would expect Yoro to stay at right-back, Dalot on the left, three in midfield with Rashford, Bruno Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo as a fluid front three?

Diogo Dalot, Andrey Santos, Marcus Rashford, Carlos Baleba and Ayden Heaven replace the injured Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo while Harry Maguire, Amad Diallo and Matheus Cunha drop to the bench.

But there’s a familiar face missing from their coverage. Clarence Seedorf has returned to the dug-out after seven years as a pundit:

Vamos juntos, professor! 👊🏾 #BemVindoClarenceSeedorf #VaiCorinthians https://t.co/XBi84HTL1z

The club have announced that the captain’s mother has died.

Manchester United is saddened by the passing of Ana Merodio Borja, beloved mother of Atletico de Madrid captain Koke and U19s assistant coach Borja Resurrección. We offer our condolences to the family at this difficult time and invite supporters to join the two teams in a minute's silence ahead of kick-off tonight.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#1334. Enzo Maresca is still searching for answers after Man City's draw with Napoli: There were glimpses of improvement but individual mistakes again proved their undoing, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026

The message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London. Clear because there is no other appropriate message to impart, really.

He has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point. The opportunity to reignite their season, to stand up, to show the Premier League they are not going anywhere just quite yet. Squads who went before them would certainly approach a fixture of this magnitude with that attitude. A squad with Kevin De Bruyne as its linchpin would.

City were still searching for answers against Napoli, a point rescued late on by Rayan Cherki. But despite the growing frustration in the stands, that unmistakable guttural desperation for just a bit more of something, it was better. More joined up thinking, at least.

An inverted full back did that for them and it perhaps should be the blueprint for the manager when they arrive at the Emirates on Sunday. City were eminently more comfortable with that; knew where they stood. Nico O'Reilly was not particularly brilliant in that position yet his presence, the safety net of somebody alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi in possession and in turn freeing up Elliot Anderson will surely make City more formidable as the weeks go by.

The set-up presented another tactical tweak for Maresca as he searches for answers and consistency. Defensively, City were twice undone by individual mistakes rather than the overarching plan, one that stifled the enduring class of De Bruyne.

A gentle hum, the half-hearted chants for a returning king, resembled an afternoon session in front of a crowd drowsy from their liquid lunches before a seesawing four-goal second half felt more befitting of City's guest for the evening, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin – intriguingly entertained by chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in the directors' box.

Rayan Cherki rescued a point late on but this was another difficult night for Man City

Former Man United striker Rasmus Hojlund celebrates his goal against his old rivals

Ayyoub Bouaddi scored his first goal for Manchester City since joining from Lille

City, sporting a fourth kit that had an unfortunate Guantanamo quality to it, certainly had more of a clue than they did here on Saturday. There were clearer patterns – noticeably Marc Guehi piercing midfield lines with one incisive pass for O'Reilly – but this is a team whose confidence has been shaken in recent weeks and that will not return overnight. 'We were aggressive off the ball,' said Maresca, while bemoaning conceding for a tenth consecutive match. 'Defensively we were good, pressing good.'

Regardless, City's supporters definitely demanded more caution thrown to the wind and some of their players wore those looks too. Anderson's dangerous crosses from that right-hand channel – the area presided over by De Bruyne for a decade – occasionally proved unsettling for Napoli, while Allan should have scored from a ricocheting corner as captain Erling Haaland claimed a penalty for being dragged down.

Man City (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 6; Nunes 5, Guehi 5, Gvardiol 6, O'Reilly 5; Bouaddi 7, Anderson 6; Cherki 7, Fernandez 6 (Ndiaye 63, 6), Allan 5 (Doku 54, 7); Haaland 5.

Napoli (4-1-4-1): Milinkovic-Savic 6; Spinazzola 7, Beukema 6, Rrahmani 7, Olivera 6; Gilmour 8; Politano 6, McTominay 6, De Bruyne 6, Lang 7; Hojlund 7.

In a sign that Maresca was placing more players in threatening areas, O'Reilly had headed over a Matheus Nunes cross – yet chances had been at a premium, those who should be protagonists taking too many safe options rather than pushing chests out and relishing responsibility.

And when there was risk, Napoli pounced. Cherki the culprit, flicking a ball around the corner aimlessly into the middle of his own half. Billy Gilmour gave thanks, punched towards Rasmus Hojlund and he spun Guehi to flash under Donnarumma ten minutes into the second half. Hojlund celebrated by shouting 'one club in Manchester' while holding a single finger aloft. 'It's good banter,' he said and we'll take his word for that.

City had been warned of the danger, when Noa Lang went clean through before checking back upon realising he didn't possess the acceleration to complete the job.

Maresca's assistant, Danny Walker, shook his head on the bench as they pored over the goal's replay. Enzo Fernandez was planting his boot into one of Vanja Milinkovic-Savic's posts when the goalkeeper nonchalantly plucked a floated cross from the night sky.

City had stirred somewhat though, helped by the inclusion of Jeremy Doku – ironically introduced seconds before Hojlund's opener – and it was the Belgian who made their equaliser seven minutes after the hour. He waited and waited inside Napoli's box for defenders to commit, finding Bouaddi alone and the teenager wrapped his left foot around the pass and was quickly racing back to halfway.

There had appeared a head of steam, only for O'Reilly to be caught well out of position as Napoli countered – City carved open – and Lang thundered a volley past Donnarumma with 14 minutes left. Cherki made amends for his earlier error by hammering into the far corner but was less than pleased.

'We played good but we don't give a lot of energy,' Cherki said. 'We need to do more, we need to win these games, and today I don't care (about) scoring my goal. I want to win this game. We're going to London to win.'

#1333. Who did figure 3? Why scientists should make experimental contributions visible

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Tito Calì is a Professor of Biochemistry at the University of Padova in Padova, Italy.

Highlighting who was responsible for each experiment could be a boost to many researchers’ careers.Credit: miniseries/Getty

I ask this question surprisingly often when reading the literature. I might be interested in a particular imaging approach, trying to understand an experiment in detail when reviewing a manuscript or simply want to contact a study author who has experience with a technique. I look at the author list, then the contribution statement, and reach the same conclusion: I have no idea who did the work.

After years of working in experimental cell biology, collaborating with other laboratories, reviewing papers and handling manuscripts as an editor, I have come to recognize that this is more than an inconvenience. By obscuring who does what in a research project, we are losing an important piece of information about how science is done — and the people who do it.

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship

This has become particularly obvious to me as my research has become more collaborative. My projects can involve advanced microscopy, molecular biology, animal experiments and computational analysis, each performed by a different group. This is one of the things I enjoy most about modern science: collaborations allow us to answer questions that none of us could address alone. But they also make individual expertise increasingly difficult to see.

When I started in research 20 years ago, papers generally had fewer authors and the experimental work was performed in one or two laboratories. Today, papers routinely have 10, 20 or more authors, with projects spread across several institutes. A 2024 study1 in Scientometrics found that the mean number of authors on papers in the PubMed database grew by more than 50% between 2000 and 2020 (from 3.99 to 6.25). Author-contribution statements help to delineate individual roles in a project, but only to a point. If five people are listed under investigation, three under methodology and four under analysis, I still cannot tell who performed any one experiment.

Anyone who has spent time at the bench knows that experiments require more than simply following the methods section of a paper.

I have seen young researchers spend months, sometimes years, developing expertise in a technique. When the resulting study is published through a large collaboration, that researcher might become one name among many, credited with investigation or methodology. But those words do not tell the person reading the paper that this is the scientist who knows how this experiment works.

For early-career researchers, that’s a missed opportunity. Publications are not only records of scientific findings, they also demonstrate technical proficiency. Being able to say, “I am an author on this paper”, is valuable. Being identifiable as the person who generated a particular piece of evidence provides a different and, in some circumstances, more useful form of recognition.

And there’s another benefit. As a reviewer and editor, I sometimes have technical questions. The corresponding author is, appropriately, my point of contact. But they might not be the person who performed or directly supervised the experiment I care about and, over time, they might not remember who did. PhD students graduate, postdocs change institutions and collaborations evolve. Five years after publication, identifying the person who remembers exactly how an experiment was performed can be difficult.

We rightly devote enormous attention to reproducibility. We record catalogue numbers for antibodies, identify instruments and software versions and deposit raw data sets. Yet we often fail to record something much simpler: who generated the data. I am not suggesting this as a way of assigning blame when something goes wrong — authorship implies collective responsibility for a published study. I see it instead as a strategy to provide traceability of expertise.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03542-w

#1332. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

“I’m really happy for Bradley, because you were asking me yesterday about him, not making the numbers,” Iraola smiled. “Also Florian [Wirtz], and I think both of them played really, really well. They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

We can look at the late switch off in due course but the only place to begin is with Barcola, who looked ready for business as early as the eighth minute when his first touch was a cushioned back heel, taking possession by crossing one leg behind the other, and how he seized his moment.

Liverpool had already taken the lead when Ronald Araújo rose powerfully to head in a Kostas Tsimikas corner but, two minutes after, the Barcola show began, a confident right-footed shot being swept past Lukas Jungwirth from 10 yards after some good build-up play from Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Koumas.

Araujo rises to score his first goal for Liverpool 🔴 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/W1C4iYd89m

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

He put his fingers in his ears as he celebrated, with every outfield player running to engulf him, and it was clear how much Barcola was aware of the requirement to get up and running, especially with Cody Gakpo, Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai injured.

Liverpool needed Barcola to deliver as much as the player himself needed to prove a little point and there is absolutely nothing wrong with having a cause to light a fire. Like a batsman who has been waiting nervously to get off the mark, soon the France international began playing his shots.

There were cushioned touches, changes of gear and even a stunned pass to Ryan Gravenberch, using his heel, that showed confidence had started surging through him and how obvious that was when Wirtz sent him scampering away in the 37th minute to finish with his left foot.

Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UJC9VW82Q8

That effectively ended the game as a contest, so it was bizarre how it ended up 6-3. Jeremie Frimpong had made it 4-0 and Robert Ljubicic’s reply in the 65th minute looked nothing more than a consolation before Barcola completed his hat-trick.

A brilliant night should have been glossed by Koumas’s first European goal – he matched Steven Gerrard in becoming just the second player aged 21 and under to assist and score for Liverpool in a Champions League game – but LASK kept pushing and exploited spaces to halve the deficit with a double from Florian Flecker, much to Alisson Becker’s obvious disgust.

Look how much it means to Lewis Koumas to score Liverpool's sixth of the night 🥹 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fLYhslbFGq

But some lapses of concentration won’t detract from this being Barcola’s night. The ambition, however, must now be to do it in the Premier League. Liverpool have invested all that money for him to do it over and over again and it would be quite the thing to repeat the trick at Brentford.

“You never know how he is going to play the next day,” Iraola said. “But it wasn’t a big surprise because we were feeling he was in a good place going into the game. He has to enjoy this.”

21 - Lewis Koumas is the second player aged 21 or younger to both score and assist a goal in a UEFA Champions League match for Liverpool, after Steven Gerrard against Dynamo Kyiv in October 2001 (also 21). Emulating. https://t.co/vmfSEaotQ9

A very entertaining way for Liverpool to make it six points from six in the Champions League. The hardest game they have left is Inter away – a fixture they won last season when badly out of form – so they have a real chance to push for a top-two finish that would mean home second legs in the knockout-stages.

This was a good night for Iraola, who was able to rotate before a tough game at Brentford. A hat-trick for Barcola and a much-improved performance from Wirtz were most welcome, but now they need to show some consistency.

Mac Allister and Gravenberch make hard work of clearing a low LASK cross, but they eventually do so. The home team have finished with a flourish and the scoreline looks more respectable for them.

Liverpool’s substitutes have not had the desired effect. Munoz is now on for Barcola, and Ngumoha has gone down with some cramp. The young wingers is substituted, as well as Nyoni, replaced by Mac Allister and Chambers.

Ngumoha too quick for LASK to handle once again, and he is hacked down at the expense of a free-kick. From there, Liverpool win a corner, which they take short and keep possession. Just trying to restore some order in the game.

The score is now LASK 3 Liverpool 6 if you are struggling to keep score. Liverpool have conceded three since Van Dijk was introduced. This was a very tidy finish from Flecker, guiding a bouncing ball beyond Alisson with the inside of his foot.

With the exception of fixtures against a select band of eight or 10 teams, these Champions League nights are becoming like League Cup ties for the Premier League teams: loads of goals, youngsters impressing and senior players in second gear.

The player who scored against Liverpool in December 2023 in the Europa League has done it again, finding an empty net with a diving header after some more loose Liverpool defending.

Denied twice by the offisde flag, Koumas has now scored his first Champions League goal. LASK were caught in possession in their left-back area, and Frimpong delivered to the unmarked Koumas who swept the ball beneath the goalkeeper Jungwirth.

Ngumoha has been a livewire throughout the game, and another shot on the LASK goal is blocked.

Then Barcola is in behind again, showing his pace to reach a Tsimikas through ball, but the winger’s dink over the goalkeeper is cleared.

That is a really well-worked Liverpool goal, with Ngumoha slipping a pass between wing-back and centre-back for the run of Frimpong and his low cross picks out Barcola at the back post for a tap-in.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

An unnecessary blot for Liverpool, Joe Gomez  – who had only been introduced 60 seconds earlier  – played LASK onside and the home side now have a goal. Gomez found himself being chided by both Alisson and Trey Nyoni.

Here come the Liverpool changes, and they come at centre-back: Araujo and Jacquet off, replaced by Van Dijk and Gomez.

Iraola opting to keep his centre-back options fresh, perhaps with an eye on the aerial bombardment that a trip to Brentford can involve. Araujo has been played at right-back domestically.

Alisson called into action for the first time tonight, and it was a sharp save down at his near post after Flecker cut inside from the right and let fly with his left foot.

The one thing that will put a gloss on the evening for Andoni Iraola is if Lewis Koumas can get himself a goal. The whole squad will be willing him to hit the target, having had two efforts ruled out for offside already. He’s provided a real lift to the atmosphere, an academy product showing you can still make the grade with hard work and a refusal to give up.

For the second time tonight, Lewis Koumas thought he had his goal only for the offside flag to be raised. Correctly, once again. Just a little too eager for his chance, but if he keeps going there is a goal in this for Koumas.

I doubt any Liverpool fans had a Frimpong headed goal on their bingo card, but that is a much-needed positive contribution from the right-back. Barcola dangerous down the left again, Tsimikas chips a cross into the box, and it was an impressive leap from Frimpong to score.

The home team moving the ball around with some confidence, but they look so vulnerable to Liverpool’s counter-attacks whenever they lose possession.

That LASK attack carried more punch though: there was an important defensive touch from Nyoni, before Lang fires just wide of the post at the edge of the box.

How many more goals will Liverpool add to their tally in the second half?

Flecker replaces Jorgensen. Iraola has decided against making any subs.

Liverpool well on their way to consecutive wins in the Champions League league phase, and the big positive is the threat offered by Barcola, Wirtz as well as Ngumoha. Wirtz looking a far more confident player, not that this is the most exacting test, and he tests the goalkeeper with a curling shot towards the far corner. There will be just one minute of added time to play.

Liverpool’s wingers Barcola and Ngumoha have just been far to sharp for their markers, LASK cannot cope with the pace on offer. The home team keep pushing numbers forward which could be a dangerous straregy.

That’s a very nifty assist from Florian Wirtz, played through legs into Barcola’s feet in the box, and the French winger’s touch teed him up for a left-footed finish across the goalkeeper. Game over, which was already the case.

What a difference a goal makes. Barcola’s touches and feints and skills are getting a full airing now and rightly so. He looks like he is relaxing and he should be aiming to score himself a hat-trick. Liverpool are miles clear of this team.

This game is a non-contest. Gravenberch lines up another shot from the edge of the box, before Barcola shows some quick feet in the box and his side-footed attempt loops over. The question for Iraola is the extent to which these performances and chances created will translate to Premier League standard.

Ryan Gravenberch so unlucky not to score with a shot across Jungwirth, which struck the inside of the far post and bounced away to safety, before a Wirtz shot deflects behind. Liverpool waltzing through the LASK defence with ease now.

Lewis Koumas thought he had scored a third for Liverpool, but the flag was raised for offside. He was a yard or two off, but it was still a very accomplished finish.

Liverpool just need a goal or two from Wirtz now and the night would be complete. LASK actually made a confident start in the first 20 minutes but conceding from a corner has deflated them.

Barcola is the scorer, but the initial danger was instigated by Ngumoha, dribbling around the outside of the LASK defence and into the box where he is tackled. The ball breaks free to Koumas, and he sets it back for Barcola to find the far corner. Liverpool now in command.

The goals have been coming from Liverpool and, really, it should be a night for them to plunder a hatful. LASK have loud supporters and the atmosphere being created is typically of one of these smaller European stadiums but Liverpool are miles better than LASK and should rip them apart. Bradley Barcola looked like a weight had been lifted as he got his first goal and you would now like to see him get a couple more – it’s certainly possible for him to do so.

The another good Barcola run is found, but his shot is screwed just wide of the near post. Barcola and Wirtz certainly more involved so far.

Diligent defending from Jorgenson to halt the progress of Barcola after a burst into the penalty area from the left. From the Liverpool corner, LASK goalkeeper Jungwirth was uncertain but Araujo could not not get enough on the header.

There really is something incongruous about seeing Kostas Tsimikas wearing the Liverpool captain’s armband. The reason Alisson doesn’t wear it is because if there is a decision that requires him to talk to the referee in the opposition area, he would be miles from his own goal and potentially vulnerable. Alisson is the real leader on this pitch for this team.

Liverpool starting to turn their screw now. First, Wirtz skipped through a couple of challenges and fired a low shot straight at the goalkeeper before Ngumoha, playing on the right, drops a shoulder and drives to the byline, standing up a dangerous cross.

Then Wirtz tries another dribble through the middle, but his shot is charged down.

Liverpool struggling to clear their lines from the corner, and Schopf scoops a shot over the bar from the edge of the area.

Nyoni then tries a difficult reverse pass back towards Barcola but overcooks it. Moments before, there was a nice touch from Barcola to bring down a switch of play.

Lewis Koumas looking dangerous again, peeling behind LASK’s defence and rounding the goalkeeper Jungwirth on the corner of the penalty area, but he was forced wide and had to settle for a corner which the goalkeeper claims.

Then LASK pour forward again after a cheap giveaway by Araujo, and the home team win a corner of their own. Lively enough start.

Tsimikas scrambling rather to deal with a cross towards Jorgensen, before Alisson puts Liverpool under pressure with a stray pass, and LASK have a corner. Taken short, and then stood up to the back post but Liverpool clear.

Kostas Tsimikas captains Liverpool tonight, not words I ever expected to type but it is a team short of experience. Liverpool enjoying all of the possession so far, LASK are defending in a 5-2-3 shape, so Liverpool’s full-backs should have some time and space. Gravenberch does well to win a foul in midfield.

The home team play in all red, so Liverpool are in their white away strip. It looks like there is some Liverpool support among the locals/neutrals in the home end.

LASK XI: Jungwirth, Jorgensen, Mbuyamba, Alemao, Andrade, Dibango, Danek, Bogarde, Schopf, Lang, Adeniran

Subs: Schutzenauer, Schillinger, Freckleton, Ljubicic, Kalajdzic, Verhaeghe, Elfadli, Flecker, Kane.

A young Liverpool team has been selected to face Linz – the third youngest, according to Opta, that the club have fielded in the Champions League – and Andoni Iraola is being mindful of players such as Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister being overburdened ahead of Saturday’s trip to Brentford.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Asked about Liverpool’s youthful team, Iraola said: “For me Trey [Nyoni], [Lewis] Koumas and Rio [Ngumoha] are young players coming in from the academy but they are first team players.

“They are first team players because we trust them, and in our situation, where we have some injuries, and we come from playing three days ago. I think they can play well, and I hope they do well.”

Iraola makes four changes from the defeat by City so in come Frimpong, Tsimikas, Nyoni and Ngumoha.

Liverpool XI: Alisson, Frimpong, Araujo, Jacquet, Tsimikas, Nyoni, Gravenberch, Wirtz, Barcola, Koumas, Ngumoha

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky

Our team to take on LASK ✊ #UCL https://t.co/8vObg7mgLF

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

#1331. Menopause can speed up brain ageing — hormone therapy might protect it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Hormonal changes during menopause could explain why Alzheimer’s disease affects more women than men. Credit: Maskot/Getty

Some types of hormone therapy for menopause are linked to better memory performance and a reduced risk of mild cognitive impairment, according to data presented at a neuroscience conference that began on 14 November. The findings suggest that some therapies could be protective against the brain changes that often precede Alzheimer’s disease, say the authors, although more research is needed to confirm this effect.

The research is part of a series of studies presented at the Society for Neuroscience’s Neuroscience 2026 conference that reveal differences in cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression on the basis of biological sex or life stage. The studies have not been peer reviewed.

Women are twice as likely to develop AD than are men. But the reasons for these sex differences are poorly understood and poorly studied, say researchers in the field. “The women’s health gap is huge,” Liisa Galea, a neuroscientist at the University of Toronto in Canada, told reporters at the conference, which was held in Washington DC. Part of the problem is that studies often do not analyse sex differences, she adds.

Researchers think that hormonal changes that happen during menopause could partly explain why the disease affects women and men differently. For instance, going through menopause early, between 40 and 45 years old, is thought to increase a woman’s risk of cognitive decline and developing AD. Some studies have found that oestrogen — which decreases during menopause — has a protective effect on the brain.

Mateja Perović, a neuroscientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, and her team wanted to know whether menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), which is used to supplement oestrogen levels and treat symptoms of menopause, can slow cognitive ageing and reduce the risk of developing AD. Perović says that previous studies have showed mixed results, but these studies had not differentiated between the different types of MHT1.

The team analysed the cognitive function of around 14,000 women who received different types of MHT or none at all2. They also compared cognitive function between women using MHT who had a genetic risk of developing AD and those who didn’t.

They found that oestradiol-based treatments — which contain a compound that is chemically identical to the oestrogen produced by the body — were associated with better episodic memory in women without cognitive impairment than were treatments containing a mix of natural and synthetic oestrogens. Episodic memory refers to the ability to learn and recall information. A deficit in this can be an early symptom of AD. Women who did not receive any MHT also showed better episodic memory than did those who received the mixed-oestrogen treatments.

Oestradiol-based MHT also showed benefits for women who were not genetically predisposed to AD and had mild cognitive impairment, whereas the mixed-oestrogen MHT did not.

Both treatment types were beneficial for other types of long-term memory function compared with no MHT for women who had mild cognitive impairment and carried a gene called APOE4, which is linked to an increased risk of developing AD. But MHT use did not affect the risk of progressing to dementia, suggesting that the treatments might improve a person’s cognitive function without preventing the disease.

When the researchers looked at structural brain changes using imaging techniques, they found that women with the APOE4 gene who took oestradiol had higher cortical thickness and less white-matter damage than did women not receiving MHT. Decreased cortical thickness, caused by the loss of neurons, is associated with decreased brain function and can be an early indicator of cognitive impairment. The findings suggest that oestradiol-based MHT might be particularly beneficial for women at higher risk of developing AD, says Perović.

Mia Schaumberg, who studies healthy brain ageing at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Sippy Downs, Australia, says it is promising that research is considering individual risk factors, such as genetics and differences in MHT composition, when looking at women’s cognitive health. “It is starting to gain the attention that it deserves,” she adds.

However, Susan Davis, an endocrinologist and researcher at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, says that the effect of MHT on AD risk needs to be investigated in a randomized clinical trial to validate the findings of this study.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03667-y

#1330. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

#1329. Marching on together, Ao? Leeds look to tie down Tanaka to a new deal after shining this season - with Dominic Calvert-Lewin also in extension talks amid Man United interest

By SIMON JONES and TOM COLLOMOSSE, FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 14:08 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:18 EST, 25 November 2026

Leeds United are in advanced talks with Japan international Ao Tanaka over a new contract.

The 28-year-old midfielder is close to agreeing terms on a deal that will keep him at Elland Road until 2029 with his current contract due to expire in the summer of 2028.

Leeds have lost only 10 games out of the 66 Tanaka has started since joining the club from Fortuna Dusseldorf in 2024. He has had an impressive start to the current campaign, becoming a key figure in Daniel Farke's side, starting in nine of Leeds' 11 Premier League matches. They currently sit seventh in the table.

Leeds have already tied down Ethan Ampadu to a four-year deal while Joe Rodon, Jayden Bogle and Brenden Aaronson all signed new contracts during the summer transfer window.

Talks are also expected to progress over a new deal for Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who has been linked with a move to bitter rivals Manchester United as they look to bolster their striking department.

Discussing Tanaka's form ahead of their emphatic win over Chelsea at the weekend, Farke said: 'It was a big ask for him after spending many years on second-tier level in Germany or here in the Championship.

Ao Tanaka (left) is in advanced talks with Leeds United over signing a new contract until 2029

Leeds are also in talks with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin over a new deal to stay at Elland Road

'Last season was his first year in the top league. I think he’d shown glimpses of his potential, but he needed to find a bit of consistency. I would agree that he is finding this during the season.

'It was not always a 10 out of 10 performance but I think it's important for a player, once you're mature, that on the weaker days you're still a six or a seven out of 10, and this is what he's doing.

'So perhaps even on the more challenging days, he's at least solid and plays first of all with good confidence, like he always does, but also with a seriousness to be consistent and to work for the team, also against the ball, strong in the duels.

'Still sometimes in decision-making and in front of goal he can be a bit calmer. But overall, I think he's on a really good path to mature more and more. And if you do this, then you become more and more important for us. And we're all happy that he is in such a shape at the moment.'

#1328. AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

As the news spread from one mathematician to the next, panic set in. On 6 October, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, released more than 700 preprints written by AI, claiming to have solved more than 300 major open problems in mathematics. Some researchers stayed up all night combing through the papers that the company had posted, anxious to know whether their entire research programmes had been rendered obsolete overnight.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Depending on who you ask, this was either the most progress or the most catastrophic development ever to happen in one day in the history of the field — or both. Either way, mathematicians realized that their profession would never be the same. “It’s probably the end of mathematics as we know it,” theoretical physicist Miranda Cheng said at an emergency meeting on mathematics and AI at the Royal Society in London in late October. Many of the papers cracked problems by combining ideas from disparate parts of the discipline, leveraging a universality of knowledge that no human could ever match — and leaving even some of the world’s smartest people feeling completely outdone.

Since then, one of the field’s greatest outstanding challenges, the Riemann hypothesis, also appears to have been solved with AI assistance. And mathematicians across the world have joined frantic collective efforts to confront challenges raised by AI’s advances, from how to evaluate and publish research papers to how to raise future generations of mathematicians. Some see the risk as existential. If mathematical problem-solving becomes mainly a machine endeavour — seen as a utility like water or electricity — then their profession could lose its status in society and human expertise might start to dwindle.

“It’s a challenge like we’ve never faced in mathematics — or in academia as a whole,” says Simon Machado, a mathematician at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich.

The bombshell paper drop in October came on the heels of earlier shocks to the field. OpenAI, which is based in San Francisco, California, released a batch of ten important results in August and, in early September, followed up with a historic solution to the Navier–Stokes problem about how fluids flow. The firm had been making noises to indicate that much more was to come. Still, many researchers were surprised by the enormity of the 6 October release. “To just see it as a giant list, without the care and thought and the love that goes into doing this work on a normal basis, it was really jarring,” says Catherine Cossaboom, a master’s student in mathematics at the University of Oxford, UK.

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms

Perhaps no source has documented the moment better than Proofs and Prompts, an online forum that publishes essays on the impact of AI on mathematics. An 8 October post titled “100+ reactions to 100+ solutions” collected immediate reactions from dozens of students and career researchers to OpenAI’s 6 October drop. Some wrote poems, others quoted the writers Leo Tolstoy and Stanisław Lem, still others posted fragments from the Gospels (in the original Greek). One contribution reinterpreted the lyrics of ‘Jolene’ by the late country singer Dolly Parton:

And I can easily understand / How you could easily take my math / But you don’t know what it means to me, AI

The tone ranged from the enthusiastic to the angry and the despondent. “Some of them made me really feel heartbroken,” says Albane Théry, an applied mathematician at the University of Warwick in Coventry, UK, who is one of the volunteer moderators of the forum.

Few subfields of mathematics were spared and some were thoroughly ravaged. “Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career was left untouched,” Fields Medal winner Hugo Duminil-Copin wrote to Proofs and Prompts. “I expected that one day we would be surpassed, and that it would happen systematically. But yesterday’s announcement hit with a force I had not anticipated.”

Hugo Duminil-Copin fears that AI will eclipse human understanding of mathematics.Credit: Chris Peus

Duminil-Copin, who is at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, specializes in the theory of transitions in complex systems — such as those that determine how information or infection filters through social networks or how metals can acquire magnetization. (OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, also in San Francisco, had already claimed to have solved a major result in this field in late August.)

Another field that bore a massive impact was the theory of groups — some of the most ubiquitous structures across mathematics, physics and other disciplines. For example, the possible ways of shuffling a deck of cards — and what happens when you revert a shuffle or combine several together — constitute a group, as do the infinite possible ways of rotating a solid object in 3D.

OpenAI’s August batch already contained the solution to a key problem on groups. Soon after its release, during a YouTube interview, Francesco Fournier-Facio, a group theorist at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, UK, mentioned two other problems that mathematicians could now attack with the help of AI. Within days, he was emailed by a PhD student in computational biology who had used OpenAI’s large language model (LLM) GPT 5.6 Sol to solve one of those problems.

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

Fournier-Facio says that OpenAI’s October dump was even more impactful for him personally. It included the solution to a problem on which he had been actively working, called the Boone–Higman conjecture. Overall, OpenAI released solutions to perhaps eight of the top ten problems that Fournier-Facio had dreamed of solving during his career, he told Nature.

But the most stunning AI result relates to what many researchers see as the most important open problem in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis, a question that was posed in the mid-nineteenth century by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, centres on whether prime numbers are scattered across the set of all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as unpredictable as it could be.

AI assistance seems to have cracked it. First, OpenAI proved a partial result, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, in its October dump. Then, on 20 November, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he had found a proof of the full Riemann hypothesis, working with Claude, the firm’s AI assistant. However, that was quickly followed by a non-AI assisted proof by Rome-based mathematician Alessandro Masullo, which he had been working on for years. “If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford.

Maynard and many other researchers are excited by AI technology. It is “quite likely to unleash a golden age of mathematical discovery”, he said at the meeting. Another mathematician, Antoine Tilloy at the Mines Paris engineering school, part of PSL University, uses the metaphor that doing mathematics with AI is like riding a dragon: the researcher is still in charge, but the dragon gives them supernatural powers.

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

But the speed at which AI proofs are emerging has already produced an immediate negative reaction. For one, mathematicians, who have long prided themselves on their field’s culture of openness, are now wary of discussing their work in public. “People are even scared to put out an abstract for a talk they are about to give on ongoing work,” says Jakub Dobrowolski, a PhD candidate at Queen Mary University of London. “Nobody wants to share new ideas because of the speed at which somebody else can take them and write a paper,” says Peter Sarnak, a number theorist at Princeton University in New Jersey.

And although established researchers say that they are both thrilled and anxious about reinventing their discipline with AI, younger generations are much more fearful. As Maynard and other established mathematicians acknowledge, the technology already poses severe problems in relation to how to assess merit when peer-reviewing mathematics work that might have been done mostly with AI, and how to train and educate the next generation of mathematicians.

“How do we train people if a good PhD thesis can be prompted out of an LLM? The response from people who are in permanent positions tends to be ‘We’re going to see and discuss’,” says Théry. “But the timescale for that could be too long for postdoc or PhD candidates who will be out of a job in nine months.”

Many early-career researchers told Nature that this uncertainty is their main source of anxiety right now. “While it is clear that faculty are working hard to find long-term solutions to the problems we are all facing, there doesn’t seem to be as much guidance on what to do in the meantime,” says Jad Hamdan, a postdoc mathematician at the University of Oxford. AI poses “more danger the younger you are, and the less experienced you are”, adds Dobrowolski. The toughest problem could be working out how to write a proposal for a research programme that might span two or three years, or more, Dobrowolski says. “Is it realistic? Now I feel like whatever I propose might just expire within a year.”

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

A UK survey of graduate students and academic mathematicians last month by the Martingale Foundation in London found that PhD students in particular are much less optimistic about AI’s impact than are established researchers. Asked if AI would “weaken their development as mathematicians”, 89% of students agreed, compared with only 68% of academics.
